title: Know the system before changing it
summary: Turn an administration request into an inventory, a hypothesis and a reversible test.
explain: A system is more than the box or app name. It includes hardware or virtual resources, an operating system, running processes, configuration, persistent data and the people depending on its behavior. Start with the useful task. Our fictional tool, Cedar Queue, records repair jobs and produces a daily work list. A healthy process is useful only if that workflow succeeds.

Inventory the details that can change your reasoning: operating-system family and version, application version, data location, configuration location, launch method, resource limits and important dependencies. Keep observation separate from intention. A document saying “version 2” does not prove the running process loaded version 2. A service configured for automatic startup can still be stopped or failed.

Distinguish three kinds of state. Configuration describes intended settings; runtime state describes what a process is doing now; durable data must remain available after it stops. Editing a configuration file may require reload or restart before it changes behavior. Restarting a process does not necessarily repair a bad configuration or recover damaged data.

Convert “make it faster” or “fix the service” into measurable acceptance criteria. For Cedar Queue, one criterion is that submitting a synthetic work order produces exactly one saved record and that reopening the database shows it. Another is that malformed configuration is rejected without replacing the last known good file. A screenshot of a green indicator is weaker evidence than either test.

Before a change, record the current symptom, scope, recent changes, candidate causes and one low-risk observation that distinguishes them. Plan the owner, allowed target, expected effect, stop condition, rollback and verification. If the system is remote, a change that breaks your only access path may make recovery harder than the original problem.

This workshop does not discover or modify your real services. The inventory and incidents are invented. Commands that really execute create their own temporary files or their own child process. Keep all existing applications, accounts, boot settings, disks and network settings outside the lab. A small controlled experiment can teach a general principle without pretending to be a complete operating-system lab.
example: Cedar Queue’s supplied record says the configured worker count changed from 2 to 20. Its operator reports a larger backlog, but the only log says a new configuration was rejected and the last good settings remain active. Do not assume 20 workers are running. Check the effective configuration and relevant runtime evidence first. A proposed rollback should identify the actual active state, not blindly rewrite a file based on the intended change.
lab: Open the supplied case JSON and mark every field as configuration, runtime, durable data or user outcome.
Write one acceptance criterion for successful work and one for a rejected change.
List three possible causes of a growing queue without choosing one prematurely.
Choose a discriminating observation and explain what each possible result would mean.
Write a rollback trigger and the exact evidence required before calling the system healthy.
Keep the plan on paper; do not inspect private logs or stop a real service.
question: A file says workers=20, but the process reports that it retained workers=2 after validation failed. Which value describes effective runtime configuration?
options: 2 according to the supplied runtime evidence
20 because the newest file always wins
Neither value can ever be known
The number of CPU cores by definition
why: The intended file and accepted runtime state differ. The supplied observation says the process retained 2.
learningGoals: Separate desired state, observed state and user outcome.
Identify the configuration, runtime and data layers.
Write a bounded change plan with a stop condition.

additionalChecks.question: Which acceptance criterion best verifies durable work?
options: The saved record remains correct after closing and reopening the data store
The service has an attractive icon
additionalChecks.why: Reopening checks a meaningful persistence boundary. A UI or process signal alone does not prove the record was saved.

additionalChecks.question: What belongs in a safe change plan?
options: A promise that failure is impossible
A stop condition and feasible rollback with verification
Permission to change every nearby system
additionalChecks.why: Boundaries and recovery decisions should be explicit before the change.

evidence: A four-layer inventory of the invented system.
Two concrete acceptance criteria.
A change record with owner, stop condition, rollback and verification.
limitations: This is planning against synthetic evidence, not an inventory, repair or performance measurement of the learner’s device.

title: Follow a path to the bytes it names
summary: Learn paths, encodings, metadata and verification through a real disposable file experiment.
explain: A pathname tells a program where to look. An absolute path begins from a root; a relative path depends on the current working directory or another explicit base. The same relative string can name different files in two processes. When troubleshooting “file not found,” record both the path and the base rather than assuming the file was deleted.

A path is not the file’s content. Names can include spaces and non-ASCII characters, and directory entries can change while a program holds an open file. Symbolic links add another layer of indirection. For this beginner experiment there are no links or shared directories: every file is inside one newly created temporary directory under the program’s control.

Text is encoded into bytes. UTF-8 can use more than one byte for a character. A text length and a stored byte count therefore need not match. Newline conventions can also affect byte comparisons. Use an explicit encoding and preserve the distinction between logical text and exact bytes when a checksum or protocol depends on it.

Metadata such as size, timestamps and permissions describes aspects of a file, but does not prove its business meaning or origin. Two files can have the same size and different bytes. A modification time can be changed or copied. Compare the content required by the task, not just one convenient metadata field.

Permissions also depend on the containing directories, identity and platform. A readable file can still be inaccessible when path traversal is denied. Windows ACLs, POSIX mode bits and mandatory controls are not interchangeable. We make no permission changes here; the safe skill is recognizing which evidence would be needed rather than applying broad permissions as a repair.

The files command writes a short UTF-8 note named work order.txt in a private temporary directory, reads it back and creates a separate copy. It reports characters, bytes, equality and the result of a harmless missing-file lookup. It accepts no user-supplied path and cleans only its own temporary directory. The exact text is invented and contains no real record.
example:
The fixture text is “café
”. In Python it contains five characters, including the newline, and its UTF-8 representation occupies six bytes because é uses two. Copying those bytes gives an equal file even if the filename is different. A same-length altered string would still require a content comparison. The experiment deliberately asks for missing.txt inside its temporary directory and treats the expected absence as an observation, not a reason to change permissions.
lab: Predict the character and byte counts for the supplied note.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py files.
Compare the read-back text, stored byte size and copied bytes.
Explain why a filename containing spaces does not need to be split into several arguments.
State how the base directory changes the meaning of a relative path.
Record what the exercise did not test: links, ACLs, shared paths and crash recovery.
question: Why can five text characters occupy six UTF-8 bytes?
options: Every character must use exactly two bytes
The filename is included in the content size
Some characters use more than one encoded byte
why: Character counts and encoded byte counts measure different things.
learningGoals: Distinguish a pathname from a file’s contents and metadata.
Explain relative paths and explicit text encoding.
Verify exact bytes without touching personal files.

additionalChecks.question: A relative path worked in one terminal and failed in another. What should you compare first?
options: The current base/working directory and exact path
additionalChecks.why: Relative paths are interpreted from a base. A different base can explain the observation without data loss.

additionalChecks.question: Two files have equal size. What remains unproven?
options: That their content bytes are equal
additionalChecks.why: Equal lengths do not imply equal content. Compare bytes or a suitable trusted digest when required.

evidence: Prediction and observed character/byte counts.
Actual read-back/copy comparison and expected missing-file result.
An explanation of path/base and metadata limitations.
limitations: No ACL, ownership, symlink, privilege or filesystem security change is performed. This is not a permission-enforcement test.

title: Start work, prove readiness, stop cleanly
summary: Observe a child process you own instead of treating “running” as “working.”
explain: A process is a running program with execution state and resources. A process identifier is a handle for observation, not a permanent identity or proof of health. A process can exist while waiting, failing repeatedly or unable to serve useful work. A service manager adds lifecycle supervision and policy, but different managers define states and readiness differently.

Separate three questions: did the program launch, did it declare itself ready under its protocol, and did an intended operation succeed? A child printing READY in this lab is one protocol signal. A PING request receiving PONG is a second observation. Neither proves that an unrelated web service, database or operating-system service is healthy.

Standard input, standard output and standard error are communication channels. An exit code conveys a program-defined result; zero conventionally indicates success, but you still need to know the contract. Warnings on standard error do not universally mean failure, and empty output does not universally mean success. Read the combination of protocol, result and context.

Use an explicit argument list rather than constructing a shell command from data. Arguments containing spaces remain one argument when passed correctly. The lab starts the same Python interpreter with a fixed embedded program and isolated mode. It does not accept arbitrary commands, inherit the parent’s credentials through a copied environment, or invoke a shell.

A graceful stop gives a program the opportunity to finish its protocol and close resources. A timeout means a deadline was exceeded, not that cleanup completed by itself. Our supervisor retains only the handle of the child it created, asks it to stop, and if necessary kills and waits for that same child. It never finds or stops unrelated processes by name or PID.

The command runs three bounded cases: a normal READY/PONG/BYE exchange, a deliberately rejected request with a nonzero status, and an owned child that waits too long and is terminated. The timeout is a safety bound, not a benchmark. Operating-system process creation can itself have delays, so do not claim a strict real-time deadline from this teaching wrapper.
example: In the normal case, the child announces READY, accepts PING, returns PONG, accepts STOP and returns BYE before exiting with status 0. The parent records the child’s state before sending commands and verifies it has been reaped afterward. The failure case exits 7 with an explicit message; 7 is a convention of this tiny program, not a universal OS error. The timeout case proves cleanup of the owned child, not safe termination of arbitrary production services.
lab: Predict the normal response sequence, failure status and timeout cleanup.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py process.
Identify launch, readiness, application response and final process status in the result.
Explain why the supplied status 7 needs the child program’s contract.
Explain why killing a same-named real application would be outside this exercise.
Record that readiness uses a local pipe protocol, not a network endpoint or installed service.
question: A process exists but its work request fails. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The operating system cannot run processes
Process existence does not establish application readiness or useful work
The process identifier is an authentication credential
why: Different health layers need different evidence.
learningGoals: Distinguish process existence, readiness and useful work.
Interpret output, error output and exit status separately.
Use a bounded lifecycle without touching other processes.

additionalChecks.question: Why does the wrapper keep its own child handle?
options: To terminate any process with the same name
To manage only the exact process it created
additionalChecks.why: Ownership and an exact handle keep cleanup inside the lab’s scope.

additionalChecks.question: A timeout is reported. What must a supervisor still establish?
options: That the owned child was stopped/reaped as intended
That every process on the machine stopped
That all future requests will succeed
additionalChecks.why: A timeout alone is not a cleanup receipt. The wrapper must handle and verify its own child lifecycle.

evidence: Actual outputs and exit statuses for three child cases.
The distinction between readiness and one successful request.
A cleanup receipt limited to owned children.
limitations: No systemd unit, Windows service, daemon, login session or external process is created or modified. The pipe protocol is a teaching fixture.

title: Budget storage without mixing units
summary: Calculate safe headroom and distinguish byte capacity from other limits.
explain: Capacity planning starts with units. A gigabyte in decimal notation is one billion bytes; a gibibyte is 2 to the power of 30 bytes. Interfaces do not always label their units consistently. Keep calculations in explicit bytes and convert only for presentation. A percentage without a denominator and measurement time is hard to interpret.

A task often needs more than its final output size. An update might require a downloaded package, an expanded staging copy, temporary index files and the old version kept for rollback. Reserve a stated operating margin as well. Otherwise a task that nominally fits can consume the space needed for logs, temporary files or recovery.

Filesystem capacity and the total sizes of visible files are different measurements. Metadata, reserved blocks, compression, sparse allocation, snapshots and open-but-unlinked files can affect interpretation, depending on the platform and filesystem. Do not invent a single universal explanation when two tools disagree. First compare scope, units, permissions and timing.

On filesystems with a finite inode pool, many tiny files can exhaust that resource while byte capacity remains. Quotas and per-process limits can also stop a write. A write error should be investigated from its actual error and relevant resource evidence. “Free space exists” does not mean that every kind of write must succeed.

The synthetic planning rule is intentionally narrow: available bytes must cover expected new data, temporary peak and a fixed reserve. Separately, available file slots must cover expected new files. These are planning assumptions, not a guarantee about actual allocation, concurrent writers, compression or quota enforcement.

Do not free real storage by deleting unknown files during this exercise. The capacity command performs integer arithmetic on bundled invented values. It does not enumerate your disk, inspect personal filenames, resize partitions or fill a filesystem. The answer should name both the limiting resource and the missing operational evidence.
example: The fictional volume has 10 GiB capacity and 7 GiB in use, leaving 3 GiB. A job needs 1 GiB final output, 1.5 GiB temporary peak and a 1 GiB reserve, totaling 3.5 GiB. It therefore lacks 0.5 GiB under this plan. A second case has enough bytes but only 5 free file slots for 20 expected files. Neither case should be “fixed” by silently discarding the reserve or deleting unrelated files.
lab: Calculate the two cases by hand in bytes and GiB.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py capacity.
Identify the byte shortfall and file-slot shortfall separately.
Describe two assumptions that could invalidate the simple plan.
Write a safe next investigation rather than a deletion command.
State why a decimal GB display and a binary GiB display can differ without either losing data.
question: A plan has 3 GiB available and needs 3.5 GiB including reserve. What is the result?
options: It fits because final output is only 1 GiB
A 0.5 GiB shortfall under the stated plan
The reserve should silently become zero
why: The full peak and reserve matter, not just the final output.
learningGoals: Calculate binary and decimal storage units accurately.
Reserve capacity for temporary work and operating margin.
Recognize that enough bytes is not every resource requirement.

additionalChecks.question: Many tiny files exhaust a finite file-slot/inode resource. What can still be true?
options: Every filesystem uses the same inode design
additionalChecks.why: Different resources can reach their limits independently. Filesystem details vary.

additionalChecks.question: Which capacity claim is most useful?
options: Available bytes at a stated time, planned peak and an explicit reserve
additionalChecks.why: A decision needs measured scope and stated assumptions.

evidence: Two unit-correct capacity calculations.
Resource-specific shortages and assumptions.
A non-destructive next-observation plan.
limitations: This is arithmetic on synthetic data, not a disk measurement, quota test, filesystem benchmark or storage-resizing lab.

title: Validate a change before making it active
summary: Practice dry run, exact schema validation, replacement and rollback on disposable files.
explain: A configuration file can be valid JSON yet invalid for an application. Parsing checks representation; schema validation checks allowed fields, types and ranges; operational validation checks whether the settings make sense for this deployment. These are separate gates. A worker count of 100000 may parse correctly and still be outside a safe supported range.

Be precise about types. In Python a boolean is related to integers, but a setting that expects an integer count should not silently accept true as one worker. Unknown keys can hide spelling mistakes. Duplicate keys can make two readers disagree about the effective value. Our bounded parser rejects duplicate keys, unknown fields, booleans where integers are required and values outside its documented ranges.

A dry run should describe the proposed difference without changing active state. An idempotent operation recognizes when the desired state is already present and performs no unnecessary rewrite. This avoids misleading change logs and repeated side effects. It does not mean the operation is automatically correct, safe under concurrency or free of cost.

For a single file, write validated candidate bytes to a separate file in the same temporary directory, flush them, then replace the active name. Under the platform’s supported semantics this avoids readers seeing a partially written destination. Atomic replacement and crash durability are not identical: filesystem behavior, directory synchronization, storage and concurrent writers need deeper treatment.

Preserve a last-good copy and define what rollback means. A syntactically valid but unsuitable setting can still require reverting after an application check. Rolling back configuration is different from rolling back a data migration or an external side effect. Never assume that copying an old file undoes every consequence of a real change.

The config command uses only a new temporary directory. It proves that a dry run leaves bytes unchanged, an invalid candidate is rejected, a simulated failure before replacement preserves the active file, a valid change takes effect, a repeated identical request is a no-op and a deliberate rollback restores the prior setting. It does not change any system or application configuration outside that directory.
example: Last-good configuration is workers=2 and queue_limit=20. The desired state is workers=4 and queue_limit=40. A typo workers_count is rejected rather than ignored, and workers=true is rejected rather than treated as 1. The interruption is injected after staging but before replacement, so the old active bytes must remain. After a valid update, the second identical application returns changed=false. The final rollback restores exactly the original logical settings.
lab: Predict every state transition before running the config command.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py config.
Check dry-run, invalid-input, interrupted-stage, applied, repeated and rollback results.
Explain what the injected failure actually exercises and what a real power loss would add.
Write one application-level validation missing from the file-only experiment.
Never replace a real configuration or add a user-supplied output path to this lab.
question: Why reject workers=true when workers expects an integer count?
options: The schema should not silently treat a boolean as a count
why: Exact type validation prevents unintended coercion.
learningGoals: Separate parsing, schema validation and operational suitability.
Explain idempotence and single-file atomic replacement.
Preserve last-good configuration when validation or staging fails.

additionalChecks.question: What does a no-op result on a repeated identical configuration demonstrate?
options: The chosen operation is idempotent in this tested state
Every external side effect was undone
additionalChecks.why: The test demonstrates a bounded repeat behavior, not every reliability property.

additionalChecks.question: Atomic replacement of one file proves what about a multi-file migration?
options: Nothing by itself about multi-file transaction atomicity
additionalChecks.why: A single-file primitive does not create a transaction across unrelated resources.

evidence: Actual six-stage configuration receipt.
Exact rejection reasons and last-good preservation.
Clear distinction between atomic visibility, crash durability and application correctness.
limitations: No concurrency stress, forced power loss, directory fsync guarantee, multi-file transaction or real service reload is tested.

title: Order jobs and bound retries
summary: Model dependencies explicitly and keep repeated work from multiplying harm.
explain: A dependency says that one task needs a condition from another. “After” can describe order without guaranteeing success. Cedar Queue’s report needs validated configuration and a usable database, not merely proof that a launch command was issued. Name the actual prerequisite state and the evidence required to mark it satisfied.

A directed acyclic graph can represent tasks and prerequisites. A topological ordering places every prerequisite before its dependent task. More than one valid order can exist when tasks are independent. A cycle such as A needs B and B needs A has no valid completion order and should be found before the work begins.

Planning an order does not execute the work. A scheduler also needs to handle failed prerequisites, cancellation, timeouts and completion receipts. Our dependency command deliberately computes only a plan and detects a cycle. It does not install a scheduler, launch background jobs or modify cron, Task Scheduler or systemd timers.

Retries help with failures that are plausibly temporary. They do not repair malformed input or missing authority. Bound the attempt count and total time, and use delay/backoff appropriate to the real service rather than hammering it. A real implementation must consider rate limits and coordinated retry storms; the paper model does not sleep or make network requests.

An uncertain outcome is different from a known failure. If a request may have completed but its reply was lost, repeating it can duplicate a payment, message or work item. Use an idempotency mechanism or check an authoritative completion record before deciding to repeat. Never treat a timeout as proof that a consequential operation did nothing.

For the toy retry planner, outcomes are fixed labels: transient, permanent, uncertain or success. Only transient may advance to another bounded attempt. Permanent stops; uncertain stops for verification; success stops as complete. The model teaches decision boundaries, not actual distributed exactly-once delivery. Later, the database exercise uses a unique job ID to show one narrow local deduplication pattern.
example: The supplied graph orders inventory before validate, validate before database and worker, and both database and worker before report. Database and worker may appear in either order. A separate cycle fixture is rejected. The sequence transient, transient, success completes on attempt 3 if the limit permits. The sequence uncertain, success must stop at the first entry for verification; it must not consume the later success merely because the answer key says it exists.
lab: Draw the dependency graph and produce one valid order.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py dependencies.
Confirm every prerequisite appears before its dependent task.
Explain why the cycle is rejected rather than broken arbitrarily.
Predict transient, permanent, uncertain and exhausted retry outcomes.
Name an operation that must not be blindly repeated after a lost response.
question: Two independent tasks appear in different valid topological orders. What follows?
options: Both can be valid if all dependency constraints hold
why: A dependency graph often permits several valid linear orders.
learningGoals: Distinguish ordering from successful prerequisite completion.
Detect a dependency cycle before starting work.
Explain bounded retries, idempotency and uncertain outcomes.

additionalChecks.question: A result is uncertain after a timeout. What is the safe next decision for a consequential operation?
options: Verify the outcome or use an authorized idempotency mechanism before retrying
additionalChecks.why: Uncertainty does not prove non-execution. Blind retries can duplicate side effects.

additionalChecks.question: A prerequisite task fails. What does an ordering-only plan guarantee?
options: That every dependent task is safe
Only an order, not successful readiness or failure propagation
additionalChecks.why: Execution gates and failure handling require more than a topological sort.

evidence: A valid dependency order and cycle result.
Four bounded retry decisions with explanations.
An uncertain-outcome rule connected to a concrete side effect.
limitations: No scheduler, network retry, delay timing, distributed exactly-once guarantee or real background task is implemented.

title: Keep a work record through failure and reopen
summary: Use a real temporary SQLite database to test transactions, deduplication and a backup.
explain: Durable state must survive an ordinary process close and reopen, not merely remain in a Python variable. A database helps organize data and enforce constraints. The exact guarantee depends on its transaction mode, journal, storage and failure model. This experiment tests normal close/reopen and a deliberately rolled-back transaction; it does not simulate a sudden power failure.

A transaction groups changes under a commit decision. Suppose completing one repair job both inserts a job receipt and decreases a stock counter. The intended invariant is that either both changes happen or neither does. If one statement fails, explicitly roll back the transaction in the application’s error path. Different database errors and conflict modes can have different automatic effects, so do not assume every error rolls everything back.

Use a unique job identifier and parameterized statements. The identifier can help recognize a repeated local request. Before skipping a duplicate, compare the relevant payload: reusing the same identifier for a different job should be a conflict, not silently accepted as success. Keeping data separate from SQL syntax is a basic correctness and safety practice.

The lab creates stock=3 and processes job-001, reducing stock to 2 and recording one receipt. Repeating the same ID and payload returns already-applied without another decrement. Reusing that ID with different content is rejected. An injected failure after decrement but before commit rolls back, leaving stock=2 and only one receipt.

A backup requires an application-appropriate method and validation. The lab uses SQLite’s backup interface to a separate file within the same temporary directory, closes it, reopens it and checks the logical rows plus an integrity check. This is preferable to pretending that casually copying one live database file always captures a consistent state.

The backup’s location is deliberately not an independent failure domain; it disappears with the rest of the disposable lab. The test establishes a functioning local backup/reopen path for synthetic data, not resilience against disk loss, account takeover, ransomware or region failure. Real plans also need protected independent copies, access to recovery keys and dependency-aware restoration.
example: Expected final state after the original job, duplicate retry, conflicting retry and injected rollback is stock=2 with exactly one receipt for job-001. Reopening the primary database and its backup should show that same state. The result “integrity_check=ok” adds a structural check but does not prove that every business rule is correct. The lesson therefore checks the stock/receipt invariant separately and records the SQLite runtime version used.
lab: Predict stock and receipt count after every step.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py database.
Compare original success, duplicate no-op, payload conflict and rollback behavior.
Check the reopened primary and backup independently.
Explain the difference between this local unique-ID receipt and a complete distributed exactly-once system.
Name two recovery failures not covered by a backup in the same temporary directory.
question: A stock decrement happens, then an error occurs before commit and the code rolls back. What should this lab observe?
options: A permanent decrement without a receipt
The pre-transaction stock and receipt state
why: The explicit rollback should preserve the tested transaction invariant.
learningGoals: Verify a multi-step invariant across rollback and reopen.
Use a unique request ID without claiming distributed exactly-once behavior.
Open and query a backup instead of trusting that a file exists.

additionalChecks.question: The same job ID arrives with a different payload. What should the lab do?
options: Treat it as the same successful request without checking
Report a conflict instead of silently accepting it
additionalChecks.why: Deduplication must not hide a changed request under a reused identifier.

additionalChecks.question: A backup file was created. What stronger evidence does this lab collect?
options: It is reopened and its data/integrity are checked
additionalChecks.why: A recoverable backup should be usable and contain the expected state, not merely exist.

evidence: Actual transaction, duplicate and conflict receipts.
Primary and backup results after reopen.
Explicit limits on failure domains and power-loss guarantees.
limitations: No production database, concurrency/load test, remote replication, physical disk failure or real disaster recovery is exercised.

title: Resolve a systems incident from layered evidence
summary: Connect configuration, capacity, process and durable data without shotgun changes.
explain: A growing queue is a symptom. Work may be arriving faster than it can be processed, workers may be stopped, a dependency may be unavailable, or a change may have been rejected. Start with the useful workflow and the measurement window. A queue length without arrival and completion context does not establish a root cause.

Correlate evidence by stable job or event identifiers and explicit timestamps. Separate a request being accepted, work beginning and a durable completion receipt. A logged “started” event is not a completed job. A success counter can also be wrong if retries are counted twice. Reconcile the data contract before optimizing the number.

Metrics summarize, logs describe events and a direct controlled test can check a hypothesis. A high average latency can hide a few extreme outliers or a broad slowdown. A percentile from a tiny sample is still only a description of that sample, not a reliable promise about future traffic. The fixture uses counts and exact identities rather than claiming performance from a benchmark.

Change one relevant thing at a time when possible, preserving the before-state and a rollback path. Restarting every component can erase useful evidence, interrupt healthy work and make the actual cause harder to identify. A targeted correction must be followed by the original user workflow and an adjacent negative case.

Cedar’s cumulative case deliberately mixes clues: an invalid proposed configuration, a healthy pipe-protocol check, a staging-space shortfall and a started-but-not-committed job. These facts have different scopes. A valid process response does not remove the storage shortage; a rejected config does not prove that all old settings are wrong. The answer should preserve each boundary.

Finish with a short handoff: symptom and impact, verified cause or leading hypothesis, observations, action taken in the lab, validation, rollback status and open questions. Label executed temporary-system checks separately from synthetic incident facts. A completed worksheet is useful evidence of reasoning, not a claim of administrator certification or permission to make production changes.
example: The fictional import fails when staging needs 3.5 GiB but only 3 GiB is available. Its error names insufficient planned capacity; the worker is ready and the last good configuration remains active. The best-supported next action is to review the staging requirement and approved capacity options, not increase workers or disable validation. A separate started event has no matching durable receipt, so the report must not mark that job completed. Real follow-up would require the authorized owner and actual storage evidence.
lab: Read the cumulative case and separate observation, assumption and hypothesis.
Run python3 labs/systems-workshop/offline_lab.py incident.
Identify the missing completion receipt without treating every absent log as failure proof.
Choose one non-destructive observation that would challenge the proposed cause.
Write a recovery validation and a stop condition.
Complete the worksheet rubric and record the next hands-on skills that still need an authorized VM.
question: A process answers PING while an import reports insufficient staging capacity. What follows?
options: The process response does not resolve the separate capacity failure
Increasing workers is guaranteed to help
why: Each observation establishes a limited property. Process readiness and storage headroom are separate.
learningGoals: Choose a discriminating test from conflicting observations.
Separate queue delay, process health and storage correctness.
Write an operational handoff with tested scope and remaining gaps.

additionalChecks.question: A job has a started event but no completion receipt in the supplied complete fixture. How should its status be reported?
options: Not established as completed; investigate its outcome
Always failed in every real system
additionalChecks.why: A start is not a durable completion. In a real system also consider collection completeness and delays.

additionalChecks.question: Which handoff is strongest?
options: A tool list with no observations
A guarantee that the incident can never recur
The tested scope, evidence, result, rollback status and remaining uncertainty
additionalChecks.why: A useful handoff helps the next person reproduce the reasoning and understand limits.

evidence: An evidence-to-hypothesis map for the cumulative case.
A reconciled job status without invented completions.
A concise handoff with scope and remaining tests.
limitations: This is a synthetic troubleshooting case supported by bounded local exercises, not a diagnosis or repair of a live machine.
